recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name the three layers and say which one you differentiate first.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Differentiate the outer sec
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the three layers before writing anything: sec outside, square root in the middle, tan x inside. The outermost layer is differentiated first and the rest is carried along as du/dx.
steps.memory_tip: Three layers means three factors in the answer, written in the order sec, root, tan — outermost first, innermost last.
lines: Let y = sec(√(tan x)),  where tan x ≥ 0
There are three layers: sec is outside, √ is next, and tan x is inside.
Take u = √(tan x). Then y = sec u and d/dx(sec u) = sec u · tan u · du/dx
∴ dy/dx = sec(√(tan x))·tan(√(tan x)) · d/dx(√(tan x))

recall.must_convey: That sec is the outermost layer, so the first factor is sec(√(tan x))·tan(√(tan x)), still multiplied by the derivative of √(tan x).
accept: differentiate sec first and carry the rest as du by dx
sec u differentiates to sec u tan u times du by dx
there are three layers, sec then root then tan
sec bayata undi kabatti daanni mundu differentiate cheyyali
the outermost function is sec so start there

steps.why: The chain rule works from the outside inwards, so the order of the factors is decided before any differentiating happens. Starting from tan x instead gives the same three pieces in the wrong arrangement and usually loses the 2√(tan x) denominator.
common_mistakes: Starting from tan x and losing track of which layer is next.
Writing d/dx(sec u) = sec u tan u and stopping, with no du/dx.

steps.label: Differentiate the root and the tan inside
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two pieces sit here: the square root gives 1/(2√(tan x)), and tan x gives sec²x. Both must appear.
steps.memory_tip: A square root always leaves its own inside under the line: √v gives 1/(2√v), so √(tan x) leaves 2√(tan x) in the denominator.
lines: For v = tan x,  d/dx(√v) = 1/(2√v) · dv/dx  and  d/dx(tan x) = sec²x

lines.text: ∴ dy/dx = [sec²x · sec(√(tan x)) · tan(√(tan x))] / (2√(tan x))

recall.must_convey: That d/dx(√(tan x)) = sec²x/(2√(tan x)), giving the final expression with 2√(tan x) in the denominator.
accept: the root gives one over two root tan x and tan x gives sec squared x
sec squared x over two root tan x is the inner derivative
two root tan x stays in the denominator
root vunna kabatti two root tan x kinda vasthundi
multiply by sec squared x over two root tan x

steps.why: The last two layers are done in one line because each is a standard derivative. Keeping 2√(tan x) in the denominator rather than trying to simplify it is correct — it does not reduce.
common_mistakes: Writing d/dx(√(tan x)) = 1/(2√(tan x)) and losing the sec²x.
Writing the denominator as 2√x instead of 2√(tan x).

insider_note: Three nested layers: sec, then the square root, then tan. Work outwards-in and keep √(tan x) as the argument of both sec and tan in the answer.
